analysis.one_liner: Creates a new federal commission to regulate large digital platforms like social media and online marketplaces.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by one senator with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would establish a Federal Digital Platform Commission with the power to write rules for online platforms, covering competition, consumer protection, privacy harms, and the fairness of the algorithms that decide what users see. It would let the commission designate the biggest platforms as 'systemically important' and subject them to extra requirements, including advance notice of their acquisitions. It also gives individuals and state attorneys general the right to sue platforms that break the rules. The bill died in committee without a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users, small businesses that sell through online platforms, and local journalism. The bill's stated goals are protecting consumers from deceptive or abusive platform practices, ensuring algorithms are fair and transparent, preventing harmful concentration of power over 'critical digital infrastructure,' and forcing interoperability so users can move between competing services [S2] [S3]. It also gives individuals, state attorneys general, and state regulators the power to file complaints and lawsuits directly against platforms that violate its rules [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, small businesses, and online users

how_it_helps.text: Creates a five-member commission with rulemaking, investigative, and enforcement powers over digital platforms, aimed at competition, consumer protection, and fair, transparent algorithms [S2] [S3].

Requires the commission to designate 'systemically important digital platforms' based on criteria like nationwide economic, social, or political impact and small businesses' dependence on the platform, then impose extra rules on them, including data portability, interoperability standards, public risk assessments of harmful content, and pre-merger notifications reviewed with substantial weight by antitrust agencies [S2] [S3].
Lets any person claiming damage, as well as state attorneys general acting on behalf of residents, file complaints and civil suits to enforce the act, and lets the commission order restitution [S3].
Exempts small digital platform businesses and news organizations from the definition, so the heaviest obligations fall on the largest platforms [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest digital platforms (social networks, search engines, and online marketplaces), which would face a new dedicated regulator, compliance costs, mandatory risk assessments and disclosures, pre-merger notifications, and civil penalties capped at 15 percent of global annual revenue [S3]. Taxpayers fund the commission, authorized at $100 million rising to $500 million per year by fiscal 2027 [S3]. Some costs would likely be passed to users and advertisers.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a powerful new regulator with broad authority over services that carry speech, including rules for 'algorithmic processes' that determine what content users see; critics of such schemes argue this risks government entanglement with online speech and raises First Amendment concerns [S3].

The bill's own design gives regulated platforms a seat at the table: 6 of the 18 members of the Code Council that drafts standards must be representatives of digital platforms, including at least 3 from the largest ones [S3].
Compliance costs and penalties on the largest platforms could be passed through to users, advertisers, or the small businesses that rely on those platforms to reach customers [S3].
The commission can 'forbear' from applying rules, and once it does, state regulators cannot keep enforcing their own rules in that area, which could limit stronger state-level protections [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real but indirect benefits: stronger competition, consumer protection, and transparency on platforms that billions of people use daily, with enforcement rights for individuals and states. The costs fall mainly on the platforms themselves, plus a new federal agency costing up to $500 million a year. The design includes genuine tension points — platform representatives help draft the rules, and the regulator would wield influence over content-recommendation systems — but the framework borrows from proven sector-specific regulators (the FCC, the FTC) and carves out small businesses and news organizations.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by a single senator, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Michael Bennet introduced the bill on May 12, 2022; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S1] [S5].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the bill's action history, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large digital platforms are better off: they never faced a dedicated regulator, mandatory risk assessments, interoperability mandates, pre-merger review, or penalties that could reach 15 percent of their global annual revenue. Senators who preferred inaction paid no political price because the bill died quietly in committee with zero cosponsors and no vote ever scheduled.

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.role: U.S. Senator from Colorado; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Digital Platform Commission Act of 2022 and made the case in the bill's findings that a handful of platforms had accumulated vast unregulated power over the economy, society, and democracy [S1] [S3].

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill; it was referred on May 12, 2022 and received no further action for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: The other 99 senators
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill or moved it forward [S4].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so support never extended beyond its author.

industries.industry: Large digital platforms (social media, search, e-commerce)
industries.note: The bill's most burdensome provisions target 'systemically important' platforms: a dedicated regulator, mandatory risk assessments and disclosures, interoperability and data portability standards, pre-merger notifications, and civil penalties up to 15 percent of global annual revenue. The industry's gain from the bill dying was keeping its largely self-regulated status quo [S3].

industries.industry: Small online businesses and app developers
industries.note: The bill exempts small platform businesses from regulation and requires interoperability standards and antitrust-informed merger review, which would make it easier for small firms to compete with the dominant platforms and reduce their dependence on a single gatekeeper [S3].

Transparency requirements around algorithmic content selection, data monetization, and terms of service could constrain the targeted-advertising models that fund most large platforms, while also giving them a formal seat in standards-drafting through the Code Council [S3].
